notes.text:
# Matthew 8 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

3. Jesus illustrates the kingdom of God through acts of healing (8:1–9:34)
      * Healing a leper (8:1–4)
      * Healing the centurion’s servant (8:5–13)
      * Healing Peter’s mother-in-law and many others (8:14–17)
      * The cost of following Jesus (8:18–22)
      * Calming the storm (8:23–27)
      * Casting demons out of two men (8:28–34)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Healings

In this chapter, Matthew narrates how Jesus heals a leper, the paralyzed servant of a centurion, Peter’s mother who had a fever, and many other people who were sick. In every case where Matthew describes what happened, Jesus speaks words, or he touches the sick person, or he does both. These stories show how powerful Jesus is. He does not need to use medicine or magic to heal people. Instead, he can just command the sickness to go away or simply touch the person. ### Casting out demons

Matthew clearly distinguishes sick people from people who are controlled by demons. Demons are evil spiritual beings who can control people. They usually use these people to hurt themselves or others. Matthew briefly mentions that Jesus drives demons out of people in 8:16. At the end of the chapter, he includes a longer story about how Jesus drives demons out of two men (8:28–34). The demons use the two men to speak, but they say what the demons want them to say. The demons know that Jesus is the Son of God, and they plead with Jesus not to punish them too much. Jesus agrees to do what they ask, but he is the one who is in charge. Again, the story shows how powerful Jesus is. ### Feasting in the kingdom of heaven

In 8:11–12, Jesus speaks about how many people will feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of the heavens. However, some people who are expected to be part of the feast will be cast outside and punished. It is likely that Jesus is referring to a feast that will eventually happen, so do not express the idea as if it were a metaphor. ## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Rhetorical Questions

In 8:26 and 8:29, characters in the story use rhetorical questions. They ask these questions to make strong points, not because they are looking for information. If your language does not use questions in this way, you could include answers to the questions or you could express them as statements or exclamations. See the notes on these verses for translation options. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

### Singular and plural forms of “you”

Most of the forms of “you” in this chapter appear in dialogue between Jesus and other people. Because of this, most forms of “you” in this chapter are singular. You should assume forms of “you” are singular unless a note specifies that the form is plural. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-yousingular]])

The word **behold** draws the attention of the audience and asks them to listen carefully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express **behold** with a word or phrase that asks the audience to listen, or you could draw the audience’s attention in another way. or [suddenly]

The man talks about becoming **clean** ceremonially, but it is implicitly understood that he has become unclean because of his leprosy, so he is primarily asking Jesus to heal him of this disease. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this idea explicit.

Jesus told the man to **show** himself **to the priest** so that the priest could look at his skin to see if his leprosy was really gone. The law of Moses required people to present themselves to the priest for inspection if they had been unclean but were now clean. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make this idea more explicit. or [let yourself be examined by the priest]

notes.quote: προσένεγκον τὸ δῶρον ὃ προσέταξεν Μωϋσῆς
notes.text: Jesus assumes that the man will know that the law required a person who had been healed from a skin disease to **offer** a specific **gift**. This made the person ceremonially clean, and they could participate once again in community religious activities. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make this idea more explicit.

Here Jesus means that the man should show himself to the priest and offer the gift to prove or provide **testimony** that he had been healed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.
The pronoun **them** could refer to: (1) Jewish people in general.; (2) the priests specifically.

People who is **paralyzed** are not able to use or control some or all of their arms and legs because of injury or sickness. If your readers would not be familiar with this sickness, you could use the name of something like this in your language, or you could use a general expression.

Here the centurion tells Jesus what is happening to his **servant**. He implies that he wants Jesus to heal the **servant**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.
The pronoun **he** refers to Jesus, and the pronoun **him** refers to the centurion. If this is not clear for your readers, you could refer directly to the people.
Here Jesus implies that he will **come** to the centurion’s house. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

The phrase **enter under my roof** means “come into my house.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable phrase or state the meaning plainly. or [you might enter into my house]
Here, the centurion uses the command form to politely ask Jesus to **speak a word**. Use a form in your language that communicates this.

Here the centurion means that Jesus can heal his servant by using a **word** of command, which is how Jesus healed the leper in 8:3. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify that the centurion is referring to a single word of command. or [a word of command]

Here the centurion speaks of those over whom he has authority as if they were **under** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable figure of speech or state the meaning plainly. or [whom I command]

notes.quote: καὶ ἄλλῳ & καὶ τῷ δούλῳ μου
notes.text: The centurion is leaving out some of the words that a sentence would need in many languages to be complete. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply these words from earlier in the sentence.
Here, the word **you** is plural because Jesus is speaking to everyone who follows him.

notes.quote: παρ’ οὐδενὶ τοσαύτην πίστιν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εὗρον
notes.text: Jesus implies that he expected Jewish people to have this kind of **faith**, but they did not. He did not expect Gentiles to have this kind of faith, yet this man did. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

notes.quote: παρ’ οὐδενὶ τοσαύτην πίστιν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εὗρον
notes.text: Many ancient manuscripts read **I have found such great faith from no one in Israel**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “not even in Israel have I found such great faith.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
Here, the word **found** represents experiencing or observing something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. or [I have observed]
Here, the word **Israel** refers to the people who live in the country of **Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language.
Here, the word **you** is plural because Jesus is speaking to everyone who follows him.

In Jesus’ culture, people would usually **recline**, or lie on one side, when they were eating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could refer to the position in which people eat in your culture, or you could just refer to eating. or [they will eat]

notes.topic: in the kingdom of the heavens
notes.text: When Jesus speaks about eating while **in the kingdom of the heavens**, he could mean: (1) that one thing that people will do is feast together. In this case, Jesus is not using a metaphor.; (2) that people will rejoice and be happy as if they were at a feast. In this case, Jesus is using a metaphor.

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, it is clear from the context that it is God.

The expression **the sons of the kingdom** refers to people who would normally belong in the **kingdom**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. or [those who expect to be in the kingdom]

Here, the phrase **the outer darkness** refers to the place of punishment in contrast to **the kingdom**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If possible, preserve the idea of **darkness**. or [into the dark place of punishment]

In Jesus’ culture, people would grind their teeth when they experienced anger, grief, and pain. If it would be helpful in your language, you could refer to an action with comparable meaning or state the meaning of this action plainly. or [grinding of the teeth in anger and pain]
Here Jesus implies that the centurion should return to his home. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

Here, the phrase **at that hour** indicates that **the servant was healed** when Jesus spoke these words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly.
The word **mother-in-law** refers to the mother of Peter’s wife.

A **fever** is a symptom of an illness in which the temperature of the body temporarily increases. People with fevers feel sick and weak. If your reader would not be familiar with fevers, you could use a descriptive phrase. or [being ill with an elevated temperature]

Matthew speaks of the **fever** as if it were a person that **left her**. He means that she was no longer sick with the fever. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. or [her fever was gone]

Here, the word **spirits** refers to the same spiritual beings that Matthew referred to earlier in the verse as **demons**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the same term in both places or make it clear in another way that these are same beings.
Matthew is using the term **word** to mean something spoken using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly.

In Matthew’s culture, **saying** was a normal way to introduce a quotation from an important text, in this case, the Old Testament book written by Isaiah the prophet (see Isaiah 53:4). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable phrase that indicates that Matthew is quoting from an important text. or [who declared]

Many ancient manuscripts read **a crowd**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “large crowds.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Here, the clause **I will follow you** indicates that the scribe wishes to travel with Jesus and be his disciple. The phrase **wherever you go** indicates that he wishes to be Jesus’ disciple no matter what Jesus does or where he goes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable phrase or state the meaning plainly. or [I will travel with you as your student wherever you go]

The word **foxes** describes land animals that are similar to small dogs. The word **dens** refers to how these animals dig holes in the ground as shelters. If your readers would not be familiar with this animal and its habits, you could describe them in general terms.
The expression **of the sky** contains extra information that would be unnatural to express in some languages. If this is true of your language, you could shorten the expression.

notes.topic: {a place} where he might lay his head
notes.quote: οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃ
notes.text: Here, the phrase **{a place} where he might lay his head** refers to a place to sleep. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a similar phrase or state the meaning plainly. or [does not have a sleeping place]

notes.quote: ἐπίτρεψόν μοι πρῶτον ἀπελθεῖν καὶ θάψαι τὸν πατέρα μου
notes.text: Here the disciple could be indicating that: (1) his **father** had not yet died, but he needed to help and support his father until he died and was buried.; (2) his **father** had died very recently, and he needed to mourn and arrange the burial ceremonies.

notes.quote: ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς
notes.text: Here, the phrase **the dead** could refer to: (1) people who have already died. In this case, Jesus is stating that **dead** people will take care of other **dead** people. What he means is that living people should not be concerned about those who have died. or [do not concern yourself with the dead]; (2) people who are spiritually **dead**. In this case, Jesus is saying that only people who are spiritually **dead** should care more about burying their **dead** than following him.

The word **behold** draws the attention of the audience and asks them to listen carefully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express **behold** with a word or phrase that asks the audience to listen, or you could draw the audience’s attention in another way. or [suddenly]
Here, the word **you** is plural because Jesus is speaking to all the disciples who are in the boat with him.

notes.topic: If it would be helpful in your language
notes.quote: ποταπός ἐστιν οὗτος, ὅτι καὶ οἱ ἄνεμοι καὶ ἡ θάλασσα αὐτῷ ὑπακούουσιν
notes.text: If it would be helpful in your language, you could turn this into two sentences, one asking the question, and the other giving the reason for the question.

notes.quote: ποταπός ἐστιν οὗτος, ὅτι καὶ οἱ ἄνεμοι καὶ ἡ θάλασσα αὐτῷ ὑπακούουσιν
notes.text: This is a genuine question, not a statement in question form. The disciples are looking for information about what kind of person Jesus could be if he can do these things.
The name **Gadarenes** refers to people from the town of Gadara.

Many ancient manuscripts read **Gadarenes**. The ULT follows that reading. Some ancient manuscripts read “Gergesenes,” and other ancient manuscripts read “Gerasenes.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

The word **behold** draws the attention of the audience and asks them to listen carefully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express **behold** with a word or phrase that asks the audience to listen, or you could draw the audience’s attention in another way. or [suddenly]

notes.topic: What to us and to you
notes.text: Here, the question **What to us and to you** asks whether **you** and **us** have anything in common or have any reason to be together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable phrase or state the meaning plainly. or [What reason do you have to get involved with us]
This is an imperative, but it should be translated as a polite request rather than as a command. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear.
Here, the command is plural because Jesus is speaking to all the demons.

The word **behold** draws the attention of the audience and asks them to listen carefully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express **behold** with a word or phrase that asks the audience to listen, or you could draw the audience’s attention in another way. or [suddenly]
Matthew refers to the people who were taking care of the pigs. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

The word **behold** draws the attention of the audience and asks them to listen carefully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express **behold** with a word or phrase that asks the audience to listen, or you could draw the audience’s attention in another way. or [suddenly]

Here, the phrase **the whole city** represents most of the people who lived in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly.
